slides.title: Process In Memory
slides.body: Process In Memory
slides.notes: First of all we will start with the Process in Memory

slides.title: Process Management
slides.body:
Process Management
 What is a Program?
Program
A program is a set of instructions stored on disk that tells the computer what to do when executed
It is inactive and does not use CPU or memory until run
slides.notes: Alright, before we understand processes, let's first see what a program is. A program is simply a collection of instructions stored on the disk. At this stage, it's inactive—it doesn't consume CPU or memory. It only becomes active when we execute it, and that's when it turns into a process, which we'll discuss next.

slides.title: Process Management
slides.body:
Process Management
Managing Multiple Programs
How does the OS actually run and manage multiple programs?
Key Question
slides.notes: Now, computers don't run just one program at a time. So, how does the operating system manage multiple programs efficiently? Let's understand the concept that makes this possible.

slides.title: Process Management
slides.body:
Process Management
Turning Programs into Processes
Answer
By turning each running program into a process and controlling them efficiently
slides.notes: So, the operating system handles multiple programs by converting each running program into a process. It then manages these processes to ensure efficient execution and resource utilization.

slides.title: Process Management
slides.body:
Process Management
What Is a Process?
Process is a program in execution
When a program is loaded into the memory, it becomes a process
Each instance of the program is a different process
slides.notes: Next, a process is simply a program that is currently running. Once a program is loaded into memory, it becomes a process. Also, every running instance of the same program is treated as a separate process.

slides.title: Process Management
slides.body:
Process Management
How a Program Becomes a Process
Once this happens, the program becomes an active process
slides.notes: Now, let's see how a program becomes a process. When you run a program, the operating system loads it into RAM, sets up the required information, allocates memory and other resources, and starts giving it CPU time.Once these steps are completed, the program becomes an active process.

slides.title: Process Management
slides.body:
Process Management
Components of a Process
Stores function parameters, local variables,  and return addresses
Dynamic memory allocated during runtime
Stores global and static variables
Executable program code (instructions)
slides.notes: Moving on, a process is organized into different memory sections. The stack keeps track of function parameters, local variables, and return addresses. The heap is responsible for memory allocated during runtime. The data section contains global and static variables, and the text section holds the program's executable instructions.

slides.title: Process Management
slides.body:
Process Management
What is Process Management ? 
Process Management is a core function of an Operating System (OS), it deals with creating, scheduling, and coordinating processes to ensure efficient CPU utilization and smooth system performance
slides.notes:
Now, once a program becomes a process, the operating system has to handle it efficiently. 
This involves starting processes, deciding when they should run, and coordinating them so the CPU is used effectively and the system runs without interruptions.

slides.title: Process Management
slides.body:
Process Management
What Is a Time Slice?
A time slice (or quantum) is a very short interval of CPU time allocated to a process
The OS uses time slices to ensure that multiple processes share the CPU efficiently
slides.notes: Next, the CPU is shared among processes by assigning each one a brief interval of execution. This short duration, known as a time slice or quantum, allows multiple processes to run efficiently without letting any single process occupy the CPU for too long.

slides.title: Process Management
slides.body:
Process Management
Multitasking in Action
Switching between executing different applications so fast that all applications seem to be running simultaneously
slides.notes: Next, because the operating system keeps switching the CPU between processes in a fraction of a second, users get the impression that multiple applications are running at the same time,even though the CPU executes only one process at a given moment.

slides.body: Process States & Life Cycle
slides.notes: Next we have the Process States & Life Cycle

slides.title: Process Life Cycle
slides.body:
Process Life Cycle
Introduction to Process States 
Process State
The current status or activity of a process at any given moment during its execution
slides.notes: Now, as a process executes, it goes through different stages. At any point in time, the stage or condition a process is currently in is referred to as its process state.

slides.title: Process Life Cycle
slides.body:
Process Life Cycle
Need for Multiple Process States
Why are multiple states needed?
CPU cores are limited, so only a few processes can execute simultaneously
Processes may need to wait for I/O operations, user input, or other resources
The OS manages these states to ensure efficient CPU utilization and system responsiveness
slides.notes: Next, a process cannot keep running all the time. It may have to wait for resources, user input, or an I/O operation, while the CPU also has limited capacity. To handle these situations efficiently, the operating system moves processes between different states based on what they are doing and the resources they need.

slides.title: Process Life Cycle
slides.body:
Process Life Cycle
Process States
Running
Ready
New
Terminated
Waiting (Blocked)
slides.notes: Moving on, during its execution, a process doesn't remain in a single state. It transitions through different stages, ranging from new, Ready, Running, Waiting & Terminated.Let's understand each of these process states one by one.

slides.notes: A process moves from New to Ready, then to Running when the CPU is assigned. It may switch between Ready and Wait/Blocked during execution, and finally enters the Terminated state when it finishes.

Once everything is ready, the process is moved to the Ready state.

Ready

Process Life Cycle
Ready State
What Happens in Ready State:
All necessary resources are allocated (except CPU)
Process is loaded in main memory
A process in Ready state has everything it needs to run except CPU time. It is waiting for the CPU to become available
Process can begin execution as soon as CPU is available
slides.notes:
Next, by this stage, the process is in main memory and has all the resources it needs to run. 
The only thing it is waiting for is CPU time.
Once the scheduler assigns the CPU, the process moves to the Running state and starts executing

Now, once the scheduler assigns the CPU, the process enters the Running state. 
This is the stage where the CPU executes its instructions one by one, allowing the process to perform its task.

slides.title: Process Life Cycle
slides.body:
Process Life Cycle
Running State
What Happens in Running State:
Instructions of the process are actively being executed
The process has been assigned the CPU
Process can continue running until it finishes, is interrupted, or needs to wait for an I/O event
CPU registers, program counter, and required resources are in use
slides.notes:
Next, during this stage, the CPU actively executes the process instructions.
It uses the required registers and resources while the process runs.
The process stays in this state until it finishes, is interrupted, or needs to wait for an I/O operation.

slides.body:

Process Life Cycle
Waiting(Blocked) State
Definition
The Waiting state (also called Blocked state or Sleep state) occurs when a process cannot continue execution until a specific event occurs or some condition is met
Wait/Blocked
slides.notes: Moving on, a process doesn't always keep running continuously. Sometimes, it has to pause because it's waiting for an external event, such as an I/O operation or another required condition. During this period, it remains in the Waiting or Blocked state.

slides.title: Process Life Cycle
slides.body:
Process Life Cycle
Waiting(Blocked) State
What Happens in Waiting State:
Process cannot use CPU, even if CPU becomes available
Process is waiting for an external event (e.g., I/O completion)
      Process will return to Ready state when the awaited event occurs
Process is removed from the ready queue and placed in the Waiting (Blocked) queue
slides.notes:
Next, when a process is waiting for an event like an I/O operation to finish, it cannot continue execution.
 The operating system moves it from the Ready queue to the Waiting queue.
 In this state, it is not eligible for CPU scheduling. Once the required event is completed, the process becomes eligible again and moves back to the Ready state.

slides.title: Running
slides.body:
Running
Ready

Process Life Cycle

Terminated
Definition
The Terminated (or Exit) state is when a process has finished execution or has been stopped by the OS/user
Terminated
Wait/Blocked
slides.notes:
Finally, when a process completes its execution or is stopped by the operating system or user, it enters the Terminated state. 
At this point, the process is no longer active and the operating system will not schedule it for execution again

slides.title: Process Life Cycle
slides.body:
Process Life Cycle
Terminated State
What Happens in Terminated State:
OS performs final cleanup
Process has completed or been killed
All allocated resources are released
PCB is deleted
slides.notes: Finally, after the process ends, the operating system performs the necessary cleanup. It releases all the resources that were assigned to the process and removes its Process Control Block (PCB), completely clearing it from the system.

slides.title: Process Life Cycle
slides.body:
Process Life Cycle
Terminated State
How a Process Reaches Terminated State:
Runtime error
Normal completion
Once cleanup is done, the process no longer exists in the system
Killed by user or OS
slides.notes:
Next, a process can reach the Terminated state in different ways. It may finish its execution successfully, stop because of a runtime error, or be terminated by the user or the operating system. 
After the cleanup is complete, the process is completely removed from the system.

slides.title: Process Life Cycle
slides.body:
Process Life Cycle
Additional Process States
Modern operating systems add two extra states to handle memory limitations and scheduling needs
Suspend Ready
Suspend Blocked
These additional states allow the OS to move processes to secondary memory and manage RAM more efficiently when many processes are running
slides.notes:
Moving on, the states we discussed so far are the basic process states.
 However, modern operating systems introduce additional states like Suspend Ready and Suspend Blocked to manage memory more efficiently. 
These states help move processes from main memory to secondary storage when RAM is limited, improving overall system performance.

slides.title: Process Life Cycle
slides.body:

Process State Diagram

slides.notes: This diagram illustrates the complete life cycle of a process in an operating system. A process begins in the New state and is admitted to the Ready state, where it waits for CPU allocation. When the CPU selects it, the process enters the Running state and starts executing. If the process is interrupted, it moves back to the Ready state to wait for another turn. If it needs to perform an I/O operation, such as reading from a file or waiting for user input, it enters the Wait/Blocked state. Once the I/O operation is complete, it returns to the Ready state and waits to execute again. To efficiently manage memory and system resources, the operating system may suspend a process, moving it to either the Suspend Ready or Suspend Wait state. A suspended process is temporarily paused and does not compete for the CPU. When it is resumed, it returns to its appropriate state and continues execution. Finally, after completing all its tasks, the process exits and enters the Terminated state.

slides.title: Process Control Block
slides.body: Process Control Block
slides.notes: Next we will learn about the Process Control Block

slides.title: Process Control Block
slides.body:
Process Control Block
Introduction to PCB
O.S.
Processes
Main memory
PCBs are stored here
A Process Control Block (PCB) is a data structure maintained by the operating system for every process. It contains all the information needed to manage and control the process
slides.notes: Now, to manage every process effectively, the operating system maintains a dedicated record called the Process Control Block, or PCB. This record is stored in main memory and contains all the essential information the operating system needs to monitor and control a process.

slides.title: Process Control Block
slides.body:
Process Control Block
Why is PCB Important?
The PCB is essential because
OS needs to track multiple processes simultaneously
When a process is not running, its state must be saved
When a process resumes, its state must be restored
OS uses PCB to switch between processes efficiently
slides.notes: Next, since multiple processes can exist at the same time, the operating system needs a way to keep track of each one. It relies on the PCB to save a process's current information and restore it whenever the process resumes, making process switching seamless.

slides.title: Process Control Block
slides.body:
Process Control Block
What Is A Process Table?
A process table is a data structure maintained by the OS to track all active processes; each entry points to the PCB, which stores all essential process information
slides.notes: Moving on, while the PCB stores information about an individual process, the operating system also maintains a Process Table. It contains an entry for every active process, allowing the operating system to quickly locate the corresponding PCB whenever it needs to manage a process.

slides.body:

slides.notes:
Next, this diagram shows the relationship between the Process Table and the PCB. 
The Process Table maintains entries for all active processes, and each entry contains a reference to the corresponding PCB.
 Whenever the operating system needs information about a process, it uses the Process Table to quickly locate its PCB and access the required details.

slides.title: Process Control Block
slides.body:
Process Control Block
Components of a PCB
A process state can be new, ready, running, waiting, etc
Contains the address of the next instruction to be executed
Contains list of I/O devices used by the process, the list of files etc
Assigned with a unique ID
Higher priority processes are selected earlier for CPU scheduling
Stores temporary data needed by the CPU during process execution
slides.notes: Moving on, each PCB stores important details required to manage a process. It includes the process ID for identification, its current state and priority, the program counter to track the next instruction, CPU register values, and information related to I/O devices and files being used.

slides.title: Process Control Block
slides.body:
Process Control Block
PCB Organization
Ready Queue
PCBs of processes ready for CPU
Wait QueuesPCBs waiting for I/O or events

slides.notes: Next, to manage processes efficiently, the operating system organizes their PCBs into different queues. The Ready Queue holds processes that are ready and waiting for CPU allocation. The Wait Queues contain processes that are waiting for I/O operations or specific events, and there can be multiple such queues depending on the type of resource or device.The Job Queue contains all processes that have been admitted into the system for execution

slides.title: Process Control Block
slides.body:
Process Control Block
What is Context Switching?
Context switching means the CPU stops one process and starts another
The OS uses the PCB to store all important information of the paused process
This allows the process to continue later from the exact point it stopped
slides.notes: Now, when the CPU needs to switch from one process to another, the operating system first saves the current process information in its PCB. Later, when that process gets CPU time again, the saved information is restored, allowing it to resume execution from where it left off.

slides.title: Process Control Block
slides.body:
Process Control Block
How Context Switching Works
Step 1
Save Current Process
Save Program Counter
Save Register values
Save current state, stored in its PCB
Step 2
Choose Next Process
Scheduler selects another process from Ready Queue
slides.notes: Next, during a context switch, the operating system first saves the execution details of the currently running process, including the program counter, register values, and current state, in its PCB. It then uses the scheduler to select the next process from the Ready Queue.

slides.title: Process Control Block
slides.body:
Process Control Block
How Context Switching Works
Context switching lets many processes share the CPU smoothly
Step 3
Restore Next Process
Load Program Counter
Load Registers
Change state to Running
slides.notes: Finally, the operating system restores the saved information of the selected process, such as the program counter and register values, updates its state to Running, and resumes execution. This rapid switching enables multiple processes to share the CPU efficiently.

slides.title: Process Control Block
slides.body:
Process Control Block
PCB Storage and Management
One PCB Per Process
Every active process has exactly one PCB
OS-ProtectedUser programs cannot directly access or modify PCBs
1
2
Key Points
slides.notes: Lastly, the operating system creates a separate PCB for every active process, ensuring each process is managed independently. Since PCBs contain critical system information, they are protected by the operating system and cannot be accessed or modified directly by user programs.

slides.title: Process Control Block
slides.body:
Process Control Block
PCB Storage and Management
Dynamic
PCBs are created when processes start, removed when processes terminate
Always in MemoryPCBs remain in RAM for quick access by OS
4
Key Points
3
slides.notes: Finally, PCBs are created whenever a new process starts and are removed once the process terminates. To enable quick process management and context switching, the operating system keeps all active PCBs in main memory.

slides.body: Booting

slides.title: Introduction to Booting
slides.body:
Introduction to Booting
What is Booting?
Booting is the process of starting a computer and loading the operating system (OS) into memory so that the user can interact with the system
Booting
slides.notes: Now, let's move on to the booting process. Whenever you power on a computer, a sequence of steps is performed to load the operating system into memory. Once this process is complete, the system is ready for user interaction.

slides.title: Booting
slides.body:
Booting
Types of Booting
Cold Boot (Hard Boot)
Starting the computer from a completely powered-off state
Example: Pressing the power button when the computer is off
Warm Boot (Soft Boot)
Restarting the computer without turning off the power
Example: Clicking "Restart" from the Start menu
slides.notes: **Next,** booting can happen in two ways. A **Cold Boot** starts the computer from a powered-off state, such as pressing the power button. In contrast, a **Warm Boot** simply restarts the system without cutting the power, for example, by selecting the **Restart** option.

slides.notes: Now, let's look at the overall boot process. From the moment you power on the computer until you log in, the system follows a series of steps to initialize the hardware, load the operating system, and prepare the computer for use. We'll understand each of these steps one by one.

slides.title: Boot Process Steps
slides.body:
Boot Process Steps
Power-ON
Bullet 1: When the computer is powered on, the CPU does not know what to do on its own, it needs instructions.
Bullet 2: These first instructions are stored in a special chip called ROM (Read-Only Memory), non-volatile, so it keeps its data even when the power is off
Bullet 3: The program stored in ROM that gives the CPU its first instructions is the BIOS
Bullet 1: When the computer is powered on, the CPU does not know what to do on its own, it needs instructions
Bullet 2: These first instructions are stored in a special chip called ROM (Read-Only Memory), non-volatile, so it keeps its data even when the power is off
Bullet 3: The program stored in ROM that gives the CPU its first instructions is the BIOS
slides.notes: First, as soon as the computer is turned on, the CPU looks for instructions to begin its work. These startup instructions are available in ROM, a memory that permanently stores its data. The BIOS, stored inside the ROM, is the first program that guides the CPU and initiates the boot process.

slides.title: Boot Process Steps
slides.body:
Boot Process Steps
Load (BIOS)
Basic
Input 
Output
BIOS (Basic Input-Output System):  A small program stored in ROM that executes immediately when the computer powers on
S

slides.notes: Next, the first program that runs after the computer is powered on is the BIOS, which stands for Basic Input/Output System. It is stored in ROM and starts executing immediately after power-on, helping initialize the system and preparing it for the next stages of the boot process.

slides.title: Load BIOS
slides.body:
Load BIOS
Functions of BIOS
tables: Tells CPU what to do first
Prepares keyboard, display, storage for use
Locates and loads the Boot Loader program

slides.title: Load BIOS
slides.body:
Load BIOS
Functions of BIOS
Note
BIOS is a lightweight program, It cannot load the entire operating system by itself, Its job is only to initialize hardware and hand over control to the Boot Loader
slides.notes: Now, remember that the BIOS is designed only for the initial startup process. It isn't capable of loading the complete operating system. Its responsibility is to prepare the hardware and then pass control to the Boot Loader, which takes over the remaining boot process.

slides.body:

On 
Self

POST (Power-On Self Test): A diagnostic test performed by BIOS to ensure all essential hardware components are working correctly
slides.notes: Next, after the BIOS completes the initial hardware setup, it performs POST, which stands for Power-On Self-Test. During this step, the BIOS checks whether the essential hardware components are functioning properly before allowing the boot process to continue.

slides.body:
POST
What POST Checks ?

Storage devices
Display/Monitor
slides.notes: Moving on, during the POST phase, the BIOS verifies that the essential hardware components are functioning correctly. This includes checking the CPU, RAM, keyboard, display, and storage devices. If these components are working as expected, the boot process proceeds to the next stage.

slides.title: POST
slides.body:
POST
POST Result
Booting continues to next stage
On Success
System alerts user with beep codes (series of beeps to indicate hardware errors when no display is available) or error messages
On Failure
slides.notes: Next, if the hardware check is successful, the boot process moves to the next stage. However, if any issue is detected, the system notifies the user through beep codes or error messages, helping identify the hardware component causing the problem.

slides.title: Boot Process Steps
slides.body:
Boot Process Steps
Finding the Boot Device
After POST succeeds, BIOS needs to find where the operating system is stored
Step-by-step process:
BIOS reads the boot order
BIOS searches for a bootable device in that order
Common bootable devices: HDD, SSD, USB Drive, CD-ROM
slides.notes: Moving on, once the POST completes successfully, the BIOS begins searching for the operating system. It first checks the configured boot order and then looks for a bootable device accordingly. Common boot devices include HDDs, SSDs, USB drives, and CD-ROMs.

slides.title: Finding the Boot Device
slides.body:
Finding the Boot Device
What is Boot Order?
The sequence in which BIOS checks devices to find the operating system
Boot Order
slides.notes: Next, to locate the operating system, the BIOS follows a predefined boot order. This order specifies the sequence in which different storage devices are checked until a bootable device containing the operating system is found.

slides.title: Boot Order
slides.body:
Boot Order
What if no bootable device is found?
BIOS displays error: 
"No Boot Device Found" or 
"Operating System Not Found"
System halts
Error
slides.notes: Next, if the BIOS is unable to find a bootable device after checking the configured boot order, it cannot proceed with loading the operating system. As a result, it displays an error message such as "No Boot Device Found" or "Operating System Not Found", and the boot process stops.

slides.title: Boot Process Steps
slides.body:

Master Boot Record (MBR)
When BIOS finds a bootable device, it reads the first sector (first 512 bytes) of that device, this sector is called the Master Boot Record (MBR)

slides.notes: Next, after locating the storage device that contains the operating system, the BIOS looks for the information needed to continue the startup process. It finds this in a special area called the Master Boot Record (MBR), which contains the instructions required to begin loading the operating system.

slides.notes: This diagram shows the structure of the Master Boot Record (MBR), the first sector loaded during the boot process. It contains 446 bytes of Bootstrap Code to locate the boot loader, a 64-byte Partition Table that stores information about the disk partitions, and a 2-byte Boot Signature that verifies the MBR is valid. Together, these components help the system locate and start the operating system.

slides.title: Boot Process Steps
slides.body:
Boot Process Steps
Boot Loader
The Boot Loader is a small program that takes control after the BIOS/UEFI identifies a bootable device
Its primary task is to load the operating system (OS) kernel into memory and transfer control to it
1. Runs immediately after MBR (Master Boot Record)
2. Boot Loader execution
slides.notes: Next, once the BIOS or UEFI identifies a bootable device and the MBR has finished its job, the Boot Loader takes control. It then locates the operating system's kernel, loads it into main memory, and finally transfers control to the kernel so the operating system can continue the startup process.

slides.title: Boot Process Steps
slides.body:
Boot Process Steps
Boot Loader
Runs immediately after MBR (Master Boot Record)
The BIOS reads the MBR from the bootable disk
The MBR contains a small bootstrap code, which loads the full Boot Loader
1
slides.notes: First, after identifying the bootable device, the BIOS accesses its Master Boot Record (MBR). The MBR contains a small bootstrap program, whose job is to locate and load the complete Boot Loader, allowing the boot process to continue.

slides.title: Boot Process Steps
slides.body:
Boot Process Steps
Boot Loader
Boot Loader execution
The Boot Loader locates the OS kernel on the disk
It loads the kernel into RAM
After loading, it passes control to the kernel, allowing the OS to start
2
slides.notes: Next, once the Boot Loader starts running, it searches for the operating system's kernel on the storage device and loads it into RAM. After the kernel is ready in memory, the Boot Loader hands over control, allowing the operating system to take over.

slides.title: Boot Process Steps
slides.body:
Boot Process Steps
System Configuration
After the kernel loads, the system needs to communicate with hardware devices, this is done through device drivers
System
Hardware devices
Device drivers
Communicates
slides.notes: Moving on, once the operating system kernel is loaded, it begins preparing the system for normal operation. To interact with hardware components such as the keyboard, mouse, or display, it loads the required device drivers, which act as a bridge between the operating system and the hardware.

slides.title: Loading System Utilities
slides.body:
Loading System Utilities
Essential Background Services
Background programs that provide essential services for system operation and maintenance. The OS loads these after device drivers
System Utilities
slides.notes: Next, after the device drivers are loaded, the operating system starts the essential system utilities. These background programs handle important system functions and ensure that the computer operates smoothly before it becomes ready for use.

slides.title: Boot Process Steps
slides.body:
Boot Process Steps
User Authentication
slides.notes: Finally, once the system is fully initialized, the login screen is displayed for user authentication. After the user enters valid credentials and they are verified, the operating system loads the user's desktop or shell, making the system ready for use.
